Kingfishers return to the Lea

By Priya Raman

For the first time since the late nineteen-nineties, a breeding pair of kingfishers has been recorded on the lower Lea, on a stretch of water that runs past a retail park, two scrapyards and the back of a bus depot. The birds were photographed in April by a volunteer surveyor who had been counting mallards and very nearly walked past them.

Kingfishers need three things and the Lea had lost all of them. They need clean, slow water holding small fish; they need a vertical bank of soft earth to tunnel into; and they need to be left alone for the six weeks it takes to raise a brood. Decades of straightened channels, concrete revetment and untreated run-off removed each in turn, and the birds went with them.

What changed was not one intervention but the accumulation of several unglamorous ones. Two combined sewer overflows upstream were rebuilt. A weir was notched to let fish move past it. A stretch of bank that had been sheet-piled in 1974 was allowed to slump when the piling finally failed, and nobody replaced it, and that accident is where the birds are nesting.

River restoration schemes across the catchment have cost somewhere north of eleven million pounds over fifteen years, a figure that invites the obvious question of whether eleven million pounds of kingfisher is a sensible purchase. The answer given by the trust that spent it is that the birds were never the point; they are the indicator that the other things worked.

Water quality on the lower Lea is now good enough that the invertebrate count has roughly tripled since 2011. Roach and bleak have returned in numbers that support a predator at the top of a very short food chain. The river still floods badly, still carries a wrack line of wet wipes after heavy rain, and still smells wrong in August. It is not restored. It is better, which is a different and more achievable claim.

The surveyor who found them, a retired signalling engineer who has walked the same two miles every Tuesday for eleven years, declined to say precisely where the nest is. The trust has asked the same of everyone else. A kingfisher tunnel is easy to find once you know what a kingfisher tunnel looks like, and the birds abandon a brood readily if disturbed during the first fortnight.

There is an argument, made quietly by people who work on rivers, that publicising a return like this one is a mistake — that it converts a fragile thing into a destination. The counter-argument is that eleven million pounds is public money and the public is entitled to be told when it worked. Both are correct, which is why the location stays vague and the photograph stays cropped.

A second pair has been reported four miles downstream and has not been confirmed. If it is real, the more interesting question is not whether kingfishers can live on the Lea but whether they can move along it, which needs the whole length to work rather than one lucky bank.

The trust will survey again in July, after the second brood, and will publish a count in the autumn. The engineer intends to keep walking on Tuesdays.
